sages.notes:
IDENTITY. This is Ahai (Achai) of Shabha, the 8th-century Babylonian author of the She'iltot: not 619 (Rabbi Achai bar Pappa, an Amora) and not the Savora Rav Achai. The Hebrew Wikipedia article titled "רב אחאי" is about the Savora (the paper's own section "הבחנה היסטוריוגרפית" separates the two); it was fetched and saved (he-wiki-rav-achai.txt) only to check this and is NOT a source of the record. His own Hebrew article is "רב אחא משבחא" (sources[1]); the book's article is "שאילתות דרב אחא" (sources[2]); English "Ahai of Shabha" (sources[3]; Sefaria links it as "Achai_Gaon", a redirect); Sefaria topic slug achai-gaon, Hebrew title "אחאי גאון" with the alternative "רב אחא משבחא" (sources[4]); the Sefaria record of the book (sources[5]) names him as its author (authors: achai-gaon).
LABEL. "(בעל השאילתות)" is the paper's own wording ("רב אחאי משבחא בעל ה״שאילתות״", also the table header). No "גאון" in the label: English Wikipedia and Sefaria call the title a misnomer and the paper an honorific (he never headed Sura or Pumbedita); the bio says so. English and Russian follow the site's existing renderings in the translated research (paper 294: "Rav Achai of Shabha", "Рав Ахай из Шабхи"; papers 349 and 616: "She'iltot", «Шеилтот»), not Sefaria's "Shabcha".
YEARS. Sources disagree, so the row is "680–752 לערך". The paper: "סביב השנים 680–752" (and its table "סביב 680–752"). Sefaria: born 680 (approximate), died 752 (not approximate). The National Library's authority record, as the Hebrew Wikipedia pages link it: 680-752. Hebrew Wikipedia: "ד׳ת״מ (680) לערך - סביבות ד׳תק״כ (760)", and that he went up to the Land of Israel after 750. English Wikipedia (Jewish Encyclopedia 1901-1906): he settled in the Land of Israel "about 752 or 753" and stayed until his death; "the exact date of his death is unknown" (Steinschneider's 761 is called erroneous). The paper itself puts the move at "סביב השנים 750–753" and says he stayed there until his death, so its own 752 cannot be a firm death date. Birth about 680 is common to all; the death year is the open one (752 in three catalogue-type sources, about 760 in Hebrew Wikipedia). The lead may prefer "כ־680–760" or the century; the bio and core idea carry no year.
PLACES. Pumbedita (resolves, city) and the Land of Israel (resolves). Babylonia is in the bio through Pumbedita. "Shabha" is NOT a place on the row: the paper presents a place named Shabha near Nehardea and Pumbedita as only one of two proposals for the epithet (the other: an Aramaic word of praise), and Hebrew Wikipedia says only "משבחא שבבבל". No new place needed.
SENTENCES. Bio 1: Hebrew Wikipedia's own two sentences ("היה מחכמי פומבדיתא שבבבל. נודע בעקבות ספרו…", "הספר הראשון הידוע לנו אחרי תקופת התלמוד"); "first known" keeps Hebrew Wikipedia's and English Wikipedia's hedge (Sefaria says "first extant", the Hebrew article on the book "כנראה"). Authorship: the Hebrew Wikipedia article says "לא ידוע מה היה חלקו של רב אחא בשאילתות עצמן - האם חיבר אותן, או שמא רק ליקט" and the one on the book repeats it; every other source (English Wikipedia, Sefaria, the paper) says he wrote it. The bio says "his book" as all of them do and the core idea describes the book without saying what he did to it. Bio 2 is Hebrew Wikipedia's sentence (it gives the appointment as the occasion, "בעקבות", on which he went up to the Land of Israel); the paper and English Wikipedia/Sefaria add a cause (a personal grudge of the exilarch) and a verdict (Natronai "inferior in learning"): left out on purpose, the Hebrew article states neither. The name of the appointee is spelled "נטרוני" by Hebrew Wikipedia, "נטרונאי כהנא בר רב אמונה" by the paper, "Natroi Kahana ben Amuna" by English Wikipedia: the row uses the paper's spelling without "כהנא" (he is not on the roster, so no link). Bio 4 is Sefaria's description of the book ("critical and highly authoritative … for subsequent legal authorities"), attributed to Sefaria. Core 3 is attributed to Wikipedia (Hebrew article on the book: "מעטות הן הפסיקות בספר שאינם נמצאים בתלמוד, אלא שבתוך הרצאת הדברים מובלעים חידושים רבים…").
LEFT OUT ON PURPOSE (paper only, or contested). (1) The 748 death of the head of Pumbedita and the succession dispute (the paper cites the Seder HaDorot HaKatzar; English Wikipedia has the dispute without a year). (2) His teacher: the paper says his master was the head of the Pumbedita yeshiva until 748, "כדוגמת רב מר בר רב שמואל" (a garbled sentence: "such as"), Mar bar Rav Shmuel is not on the roster; no teacher is stated by Hebrew Wikipedia, English Wikipedia or Sefaria. (3) That Natronai was his pupil: the paper says "תלמידו ומשמשו", Sefaria "Achai's pupil", Hebrew Wikipedia only "כפוף"; the bio says "כפוף". (4) The paper's section on the "עיזא כרכוז" ruling and "היזהרו ברבינו אחאי, שמאיר עיני גולה הוא": Hebrew Wikipedia ("רב אחאי") tells this of the Savora/Amora Rav Achai, while the paper uses it as an example of the standing of Ahai of Shabha; not used. (5) The origin of "משבחא". (6) The paper's claims that the Rishonim "quote" the Sheiltot (Rashi, Rashbam, Tosafot, Rif, Rambam, Ramban, Rav Sherira, Rav Hai): a citing of a book, not a relation between persons, so not recorded as links; if the lead wants them, the sentence is "רב שרירא גאון, רב האי גאון, רש״י, רשב״ם, בעלי התוספות, הרי״ף, הרמב״ם והרמב״ן מרבים לצטט את השאילתות" (roster ids 21, 25, 594, 41 and others). (7) The editions and commentaries (Venice 1546, Sheilat Shalom, the Netziv's Haamek Sheilah, Mirsky, Brody) are in the tags only ("העמק שאלה"), not in the sentences.
LINKS. No roster sage is stated as his teacher, student or relative by any source (Natronai, Mar bar Rav Shmuel, Shimon Kayyara and the Netziv are not on the roster), so paper_links is empty. One influence link 680 -> 685, resting on the paper alone: "ספר הלכות פסוקות המיוחס לרב יהודאי גאון … נשענו באופן נרחב על הניתוחים המשפטיים והפסקים המובאים בשאילתות". It is a relation through a book that the paper itself calls "attributed" to Yehudai; the Hebrew Wikipedia article on Yehudai (saved: he-wiki-yehudai-gaon-context.txt, not a source of this record) says "על פי חלק מן החוקרים" he wrote the Halakhot Pesukot, calls him "הגאון הראשון שהחל בחיבור קובצי הלכה לאחר חתימת התלמוד" and says the same exilarch moved him from Pumbedita to Sura, and its section on Halakhot Gedolot reports an argument that Rav Yehudai bar Nachman "מוזכר בספר השאילתות של רב אחאי משבחא". The Yehudai paper (685) does not repeat the claim. The lead should keep this link only if it is content with a book-mediated, paper-only influence, and decide with the 685 fragment (a link in the other direction or none there).
YAHRZEIT. None: the paper gives no Hebrew day or month of his death (only "עד יום מותו"); the Hebrew and English Wikipedia give none.
SLIPS IN THE PAPER (copied as they are; the Drive text and the converted text keep them): "ההההדיר" ("פרופ' שמואל קלמן מירסקי ההההדיר מהדורה ביקורתית"); "בשקקנות" (probably "בשקדנות"); "מכרזת" ("השפעה מכרזת", probably "מכרעת"); "ומשנון שבעל פה" (probably "ושינון"); "במישור ההלכתי הפסוק" (probably "הפסקי" or "הפסיקתי"); "נבחי תורה שבעל פה" (possibly "נבכי"); and the sentence on his teacher, "כדוגמת רב מר בר רב שמואל", which does not parse. The paper's own dates do not fit each other: it gives his life as "סביב השנים 680–752" but his move to the Land of Israel as "סביב השנים 750–753" with "פעל בה עד יום מותו".
DRIVE. The owner's Drive holds one paper on him (the 680 paper, created 2026-10-18); the other Drive hits for his name are the two earlier papers on Rabbi Achai bar Pappa (619), the Yehudai paper (685) and data dumps (research.json, drive-research-import, shg_wiki_17.json, 294.json and similar); none read, none attributable to this sage. The episode (title, cover, the list of sources the owner's episode was made from) is saved as episode.txt; the list is a set of leads, nothing in the record rests on it. This record's paper text is byte-identical to the second independent copy (cmp of papers_raw/680.a.md and 680.b.md). LEAD (2026-10-27): the link 680 -> 685 is dropped (the second reader: the paper only says a book attributed to Yehudai relied on the Sheiltot, which is no relation between the two men; no page supports it). 680 therefore has no recorded link. "Babylonian Aramaic" is now "Aramaic" because the sources disagree which Aramaic (Hebrew Wikipedia reports Ginzberg against Epstein; English Wikipedia says the place of composition is unclear); the tag `ארמית בבלית` is dropped with it, since the vocabulary has no `ארמית` piece.

sages.notes:
Years: the sources agree, so the row is exact: 1806-1874. Hebrew Wikipedia: born 25 Shevat 5566 (1806), died 10 Iyar 5634 (1874); English Wikipedia (the Komarno dynasty page): born 13 February 1806, died 28 April 1874 (the two calendars match); Sefaria: birth 1806 and death 1874, neither marked approximate; Wikidata: 1806 and 1874 (year precision). The English and Russian sentence on the diary says "in the 1950s" for the Hebrew "בשנות החמישים": both Hebrew Wikipedia and Sefaria give the decade and no year, so a decade is all that is stated. Era: most of the roster's Hasidic masters of this period are filed as acharonim (587 Sadilkov, 589 Nathan of Breslov, 501 and 502 of Chabad, 129 Gur, 131 Sochatchov; 203 Gutmacher, a kabbalist of 1796-1874, too); 117, Tzadok HaKohen of Lublin, is the exception (modern). The era cell is therefore "אחרונים" and the years sit in the years cell, as in their rows.
Label and spelling: the label is the owner's own title of the episode, "רבי יצחק אייזיק מקומרנא". The sources spell the town several ways: קומרנא (Hebrew Wikipedia in "חסידות קומרנא", Sefaria's alternative title "אדמו"ר מקומרנא", the owner), קומרנה (the dynasty article's title and the first sentence of his own article), קומרנו (his article: "בעירו של אביו, קומרנו"), קאמארנא / קאמרנא (the dynasty article, Wikidata's description). The row, the bio and the tags use קומרנא throughout. Hebrew Wikipedia names him "רבי יצחק אייזיק יהודה יחיאל ספרין" (the article's title is "יצחק אייזיק ספרין"; according to the dynasty article he was the first to use the name Safrin, after the town of his grandfather, in place of Eichenstein). No page I saved calls him "בעל היכל הברכה" or gives another epithet, so the label has none. English and Russian labels follow the roster's "Rabbi Yitzchak Eizik X" and "Рабби Ицхак Айзик X" (493, 447).
Which Komarno: the Hebrew dynasty article says "העיירה קומרנה שבגליציה המזרחית, כיום במערב אוקראינה"; English Wikipedia: "Komarno, Ukraine"; Sefaria: death place Komarno, Ukraine; Wikidata: death place Komarno (city of Ukraine). It is not Komarom/Komarno on the Danube. The coordinates are those of the English Wikipedia article "Komarno, Ukraine" (Lviv oblast).
Places in the row, in the sources' words: קומרנא (he lived there to the end of his life; the dynasty's seat); פינצ׳וב (after his marriage he moved to the town where his father-in-law served as rabbi; Hebrew Wikipedia writes "פינצ'וב", the dynasty article "הפולנית פינטשוב"; identified as Pińczów, Poland, because the Hebrew Wikipedia article on that town lists "רבי אברהם מרדכי מפינטשוב" among its Hasidic rebbes, the name of the father-in-law); זידיטשוב (the dynasty article: "זמן מה שימש רבי יצחק אייזיק כדיין בזידיטשוב"; he was also raised by his uncle "מזידיטשוב"; the town is Zhydachiv, Ukraine, where the Hebrew Wikipedia article says the Zidichov Hasidic group operated). None of the three resolves in the site's gazetteer today, so they are declared in new_places with the coordinates the English Wikipedia API gives. Left out of the row: Sambir, which Sefaria and Wikidata give as his birth place (neither Hebrew article says where he was born). Left out of the bio: the father's rabbinic posts, because the sources disagree (his article: "רב בזידיטשוב ובקומרנו"; the dynasty article: rabbi of Zhuravno and then of Komarno); the bio says only that he was the founder's son.
Left out on purpose: the statement of his son (in the introduction to Zohar Chai) that he was a reincarnation of the Yenuka of the Zohar, the Ari, the Baal Shem Tov and the Gaon of Vilna, and his own statement in Megilat Setarim that he was born in the year of Mashiach ben Yosef (the dynasty article reports both as what was written, not as facts); his reputation as a wonder-worker ("בעל מופתים") and as "אדמו"ר לאלפים"; his removal from the post of dayan in Zidichov and the hardships after it; his successors and sons-in-law (not on the roster); about ten more of his books; the claim in the owner's episode title that he "refused to change even a single word": no page I saved says it, so it is not used (Hebrew Wikipedia describes Heichal HaBeracha as a commentary "בדגש על פירוש המסורה", which is all the core idea says). The episode description lists the 20 sources the owner's episode was made from (auction catalogues with sets of Heichal HaBeracha, the HaMichlol article, an essay by Rachel Elior on the Ben-Yehuda Project, pages of Sifrei Chaim, and an owner Markdown document): leads only, nothing is taken from it. HaMichlol, Wikisource and Yiddish Wikipedia could not be reached from this environment.
Links: the Baal Shem Tov (558) to him, influence (Sefaria: "אותו הוא החשיב כמורו ורבו על אף שנולד אחר פטירתו"; the dynasty article: "החשיב את עצמו כמעט כתלמידו הישיר של הבעש"ט אף שהיה כמה דורות אחריו"): influence and not teacher, since both say he was born after the Baal Shem Tov's death. The Ari (462) to him, influence (Hebrew Wikipedia: in his books he combined "קבלת האר"י ותורת הבעש"ט"). His teachers named by Hebrew Wikipedia (Avraham Yehoshua Heshel of Apta, his uncle Zvi Hirsch of Zidichov, Naftali Zvi of Ropshitz, Moshe Zvi of Savran, Asher Yeshaya Rubin of Ropshitz), his father Alexander Sender and his father-in-law Avraham Mordechai are not on the roster, so no teacher or family link can be recorded; the quotes are in the saved Hebrew Wikipedia page should one of them join. He is not 447 (Rabbi Yitzchak Eizik Tyrnau) and not 493 (Rabbi Yitzchak Eizik Chaver).
No owner paper (the Drive holds none on him), so there are no paper-link candidates and no yahrzeit candidate. His day of death, 10 Iyar 5634, is given by Hebrew Wikipedia and the dynasty article, but the death-date file takes dates from papers only.
Spelling: book titles in English follow Sefaria (Heichal HaBeracha, Zohar Chai, Shulchan HaTahor, Megilat Setarim); Russian town names follow the Hasidic usage (Зидичов, Ропшиц, Савран, Апта), except Pińczów (Пинчув). LEAD (2026-10-27): Pińczów in Russian is «Пиньчув» (Russian Wikipedia's name, Wikidata Q275592), in the sentence and in the vocabulary. The diary "kept secret until the middle of the twentieth century" (his own Hebrew Wikipedia article), not "until the twentieth century" (Sefaria).

sages.notes:
NOT 626 (Rabbi Nathan Shapira of Jerusalem, "HaNasi"): 626 is the nephew of this sage. Hebrew Wikipedia on 626 says "דודו, גם הרב נתן נטע שפירא, היה מפורסם ונקרא בשם המגלה עמוקות", and the research paper already on the site for 626 says "ודודו היה המקובל המפורסם רבי נתן נטע שפירא, מחבר הספר מגלה עמוקות". Recorded as a family link 682 -> 626 (relation uncle), sourced from Hebrew Wikipedia's article on 626 (sources[4]). The paper of 626, not the paper of 682, states it, and the validator accepts paper-link candidates only for the fragment's own paper, so it is not in paper_links: the lead may add it to data/links-from-research.json as an entry of paper 626 (paper "626", a "682", b "626", relation "uncle", quote from public/research/626.json: ודודו היה המקובל המפורסם רבי נתן נטע שפירא, מחבר הספר "מגלה עמוקות").

YEARS. The sources disagree on the birth year: Hebrew Wikipedia "ה'שמ"ה, ~ 1584"; the owner's paper "ה'שמ"ה, 1584/1585 בקירוב" (5345 runs from autumn 1584 to autumn 1585); English Wikipedia and Sefaria 1585 (Sefaria's birthYearIsApprox is false, but the paper's own source list quotes the National Library of Israel record as "approximately 1585-1633"). Death is agreed: 13 Av 5393 = 20 July 1633 (the paper and Hebrew Wikipedia; English Wikipedia 20 July 1633; Sefaria 1633; the conversion of 13 Av 5393 to 20 July 1633 was checked with the Hebrew calendar). The row says כ־1585–1633 (the birth is approximate, as the National Library's wording and the paper's "בקירוב" say); the bio and the core idea give no birth or death year. The other years in the bio come from the sources: 1608 (the move to Kazimierz: "בערך" in Hebrew Wikipedia, "סביב" in the paper) and 1617 (the appointment: the paper "כבן שלושים ואחת בלבד", Hebrew Wikipedia "בן שלושים ואחת"). 252 is the number of ways in the book, not a year.

OFFICE. English Wikipedia and Sefaria call him "Chief Rabbi of Kraków". Hebrew Wikipedia and the paper say he was appointed head of the yeshiva and preacher (ראש ישיבה ודרשן) of the Kraków community, and the paper says that at the time the Bach (Rabbi Yoel Sirkis, 76) was the city's rabbi and head of the court. The bio follows Hebrew Wikipedia and the paper; "chief rabbi" is not written.

PLACES. Born in Hrodna is the paper's statement ("הוא נולד בעיר הורדנה (גרודנא)"); Hebrew Wikipedia says only that he moved from Hrodna to Kazimierz about 1608, and English Wikipedia and Sefaria give no birthplace (Sefaria gives Krakow as the place of death). Spelling: the sources write הורדנה; the gazetteer has the same city as גרודנה (53.68, 23.83) but no entry for הורדנה, so it is declared in new_places with the coordinates the Wikipedia API gives for the article "Grodno" (53.667, 23.833); the lead may alias it to the existing point instead. Kraków is written קרקוב (Hebrew Wikipedia's spelling and the one the gazetteer knows; the owner's episode and paper spell it קראקא, as sage 626's row does, which the map does not resolve). Kraków comes first as the place where he worked and the map pin. Kazimierz, where he lived (a place by Kraków, "קז'ימייז' שעל יד קראקא"), is not a separate piece.

THE BOOKS. "Fifteen books, seven of them on the Torah" is written "according to his son's testimony in the preface to his book", as the paper attributes it (Hebrew Wikipedia states it flatly). "252 ways" is in Hebrew Wikipedia, in Sefaria's description and in the paper (the owner's episode title says it too). The paper's table of works gives printing places and years (Kraków 5397/1637 for the Va'etchanan book, Lublin 5383/1623 for the Zohar commentary, Zalkow 5555/1795 for the work on the whole Torah); Hebrew Wikipedia gives the same for the first two. None of it is in the bio.

TEACHERS. English Wikipedia ("A student of Meir Lublin"), Sefaria (a teacher link to the Maharam of Lublin, slug maharam-lublin) and the paper (naming the Maharam of Lublin, citing the National Library) give the Maharam of Lublin (Rabbi Meir ben Gedaliah) as his teacher; Hebrew Wikipedia and the paper say he received guidance in the mysteries of Kabbalah from Rabbi Moshe Mordechai Margaliot, whom he replaced as head of the yeshiva. Neither is on the roster (no sage there is the Maharam of Lublin or Margaliot of Kraków; 453 and 480 are other Margaliots), so no teacher link is recorded. His father Shlomo, his grandfather Nata Shapira the First and his father-in-law are not on the roster either.

LINKS RECORDED. (1) teacher 682 -> 83 (the Shach): Hebrew Wikipedia "גדול תלמידיו היה רבי שבתי כהן"; Hebrew Wikipedia on the Shach "והיה לומד בילדותו אצל המגלה עמוקות"; Sefaria lists the Shach as his student; the paper lists him among the main students and says "הש"ך קיבל מרבו את היסודות" (a paper-link candidate). To look at: the Shach was born in 1622 (Hebrew Wikipedia; the roster has 1622) and Nata died in 1633, so the Shach was a child, which is what his own article says ("בילדותו"). (2) family 682 -> 626, uncle (above). (3) family 682 -> 653 (Rabbi Yehonatan Eybeschutz), relation ancestor: Hebrew Wikipedia lists him under "מצאצאיו"; the paper says of Nata's daughter Devorah and her husband "ונינם היה הגאון רבי יהונתן אייבשיץ" (a paper-link candidate), that is, a great-grandson of that couple. The pages disagree on which daughter married which Yeshaya (the paper: Devorah to Rabbi Yeshaya Ashkenazi, head of the court of Kovla, and Lifsha to Rabbi Yeshaya of Hildesheim; Hebrew Wikipedia: Devorah to Rabbi Yeshaya Hildesheim Ashkenazi of Kraków, and Lifsha Simcha to Israel Heilprin of Kerstein); both put Eybeschutz among his descendants. (4) influence 462 (the Ari) -> 682: the paper says the teaching of the Ari came to the Polish centre and that Rabbi Nata "שימש חוליה מרכזית בקליטתה, בניסוחה מחדש ובשילובה של הקבלה הלוריאנית", and English Wikipedia says he "played an important role in spreading Isaac Luria's teachings throughout Poland" (Hebrew Wikipedia adds that he took on Tikkun Chatzot). The lead may drop this one if it is thought too general; the other three are explicit.

SEEN, NOT RECORDED AS LINKS. The Bach (76) was the rabbi of Kraków at the same time (the paper: "באותה תקופה שימש הגאון רבי יואל סירקיש ... כרב העיר", and "the combination" of the two made Kraków a centre): the paper does not call them colleagues, so there is no colleague link. Chaim Vital (542) and Israel Sarug appear in the paper only as authors of the Lurianic writings that spread elsewhere, in contrast to his sermons. The other students and descendants named in the paper and in Hebrew Wikipedia are not on the roster: Berachia Berakh, Noach of Pinsk, Yehoshua Heschel Zoref, Pinchas Shapira of Koretz, Shmuel HaLevi Kelin, Chaim Halberstam of Sanz, Shlomo Rabinowitz of Radomsk, Meir Shapiro of Lublin, Liber the Great of Berditchev, Mordechai of Neshchiz, Menachem Mendel of Rimanov, Aryeh Leib Zunz, Tzvi Elimelech of Dinov (who interpreted the Megaleh Amukot in Agra DeKalla: Hebrew Wikipedia and the paper). The roster's Rabbi Eliyahu Shapira (648) is not named as a descendant by any of the pages saved. The sons-in-law (Naftali Zvi Hirsch Shor, Yeshaya Ashkenazi and others) are not on the roster.

LEFT OUT ON PURPOSE (given by the sources as a tradition, a legend or a family lineage): his descent "על פי המסורת המשפחתית" from Rashi, Rabbi Shimshon Shapira of Pozna, Rabbi Nathan ben Yechiel of Rome and King David (the paper) and "ייחוסו מגיע עד לרש"י" (Hebrew Wikipedia); the tombstone's text that Elijah spoke with him face to face, which the paper and Hebrew Wikipedia give as what was said about him ("הוא שאומרים עליו"); the heavenly voice that stopped him at 252 (the paper "לפי המסורת", Hebrew Wikipedia "ע"פ המסורת"); the legend of the stone "יגיד עליו רעו" and of the stranger buried beside him; the story of the man in a hair cloak who appeared at Tikkun Chatzot. The paper's evaluations ("אחת הדמויות המרכזיות והמשפיעות ביותר", "קו פרשת מים", a synthesis "חסרת תקדים") are not repeated: the core idea has only the plain statement of English Wikipedia, which the paper's description of his role in the Ari's teaching supports. His wealth and his father-in-law's support (the paper: a synagogue, a study house and a mikveh built for him), and that he took no salary (English Wikipedia; Hebrew Wikipedia "שלא על מנת לקבל פרס"), were left out for length.

CHILDREN. Hebrew Wikipedia lists ten children; English Wikipedia seven (three sons, four daughters), and the paper names three sons and four daughters. No number is written. His son Rabbi Shlomo, who published the book (died at 32 according to the paper and Hebrew Wikipedia), is not on the roster.

THE PAPER (Drive: Google Doc 1YXwErMDJNSUjasevIdlNYAv0QuFT7h4EfSfMYKym6F8, created 2026-10-18; copied to W/papers_raw/682.a.md and converted to W/papers/682.txt). It is about this sage. Slips and doubtful points in the Drive text, copied as they are (a list for the owner): "שני רבות מובהקים" (the noun does not agree: "רבים"); "ומורת יוטל נישאה לרבי מנחם מנדל" ("ומורת" for "ומרת"); the marriages of the daughters (above) differ from Hebrew Wikipedia's; the Maharam of Lublin as his teacher rests in the paper on one citation, the National Library record ([cite: 2]); the first paragraph and the closing paragraphs are evaluations ("אחת הדמויות המרכזיות והמשפיעות ביותר"); source 6 has typographic quotation marks inside "י”ג אב שצ”ג". No Arabic letters and no markdown debris after conversion.

DRIVE. The only document in the owner's Drive whose title names him is this paper; a full-text search for "מגלה עמוקות" finds mentions in the owner's papers on other sages (the Rokeach, the Shach, the Shelah), not a second document on him.

EPISODE. The owner's episode title says "המקובל שגילה 252 סודות בתפילה אחת של משה רבינו"; the bio says only what the sources say (252 ways to explain one prayer of Moses). core_idea.he: בנבואת ירמיהו היא האם הבוכה על בניה: ״רחל מבכה על־בניה מאנה להנחם על־בניה כי איננו״, ובפסוק הבא נאמר ״מנעי קולך מבכי ועיניך מדמעה כי יש שכר לפעלתך״.
core_idea.en: In Jeremiah’s prophecy she is the mother weeping for her children: “Rachel weeping for her children, refusing to be comforted for her children, for they are not”, and the next verse says: “Restrain your voice from weeping and your eyes from tears, for there is reward for your work”.
core_idea.ru: В пророчестве Йирмияху она — мать, плачущая о своих детях: «Рахель плачет о детях своих, не хочет утешиться о детях своих, потому что их нет», а в следующем стихе сказано: «Удержи голос свой от плача и глаза свои от слёз, ибо есть награда за труд твой».

core_idea.en: According to Rashi, Jacob buried her on the road “by the divine word”, so that she would be “a help to her children” when Nebuzaradan exiled them: “Rachel goes out upon her grave, weeping and pleading for mercy for them”.
core_idea.ru: По Раши, Яаков похоронил её на дороге «по слову Всевышнего», чтобы она была «помощью детям своим», когда Невузарадан уведёт их в изгнание: «Рахель выходит на свою могилу, плачет и молит о милосердии для них».

sages.notes: No years: like Leah's row (613) the years cell is “תקופת האבות” and no source gives a date, so the record carries none and the bio and core idea carry no year. The Hebrew Wikipedia also says, from sources outside the Bible, that she was 36 at her death: left out (a number the Torah does not give). Primary source: the Torah text through Sefaria (Genesis 29, 30, 35; Jeremiah 31; Ruth 4), quoted verbatim in the Masoretic spelling (with maqaf), saved in full under sources/683. What the Sages say is attributed to them: the Talmud (Megillah 13b) and Rashi (on Genesis 29:25, 30:22, 48:7); Rashi's words on Genesis 48:7 are Jacob's explanation to Joseph in Rashi's reading and are given as Rashi's, not as fact. In the Hebrew sentence the quoted word is Rashi's own spelling “הדבור” (the divine word). Jeremiah 31:15 is the verse of Rachel weeping in the Masoretic numbering (Sefaria 31:15); the Hebrew Wikipedia cites it as 31:14. The answer “מנעי קולך מבכי” is the next verse (31:16); who is addressed is not named in the verse and the sentence does not say. The Sefaria topic page and the Hebrew Wikipedia say she is 'one of the four matriarchs'; the Torah text does not use the term. Left out on purpose: the midrash that Leah and Rachel were twins and that Leah was to marry Esau (Hebrew Wikipedia: 'according to various midrashim'); the claim that the silence passed to Benjamin and Esther (Hebrew Wikipedia marks it [דרוש מקור]); Rachel and the teraphim (Genesis 31:19, 34-35) and the commentators' reasons for it; the dispute between commentators on the site of her grave (Hebrew Wikipedia: the Bethlehem tomb or a grave north of Jerusalem; 1 Samuel 10:2) - the bio gives only the verse; the date of her death: Hebrew Wikipedia gives 11 Cheshvan ('according to the various midrashim', Yalkut Shimoni, from the Book of Jubilees) and the Pesikta Rabbati 'between Pesach and Shavuot', and a scholar's view that the Yalkut means Iyar: sources disagree and none is the Torah, so no yahrzeit is recorded (the sage has no paper). Place: Genesis 35:19 and 48:7 give “בדרך אפרת הוא בית לחם” and “בארץ כנען”; Genesis 29:4-6 place her in Haran. The location cell names בית לחם first, where she is buried (the first place named at the same level is the map point, so her marker stands in the Land of Israel with Jacob, Isaac, Rebecca and Sarah, and agrees with the region), then Leah's form for the rest (פדן ארם (חרן); ארץ כנען; Leah's row names Haran first). No keyword of lib/regions.ts matches any of the three (Leah's row gets its region from חברון), so the validator found no region: בית לחם is declared in new_places with region eretz-israel (its map point already exists in lib/locationCoords.ts). Adding that keyword to lib/regions.ts also changes the derived region of 535 (צרויה, location “בית לחם; ממלכת דוד”) from none to eretz-israel: the lead decides. Links: Jacob (husband) from Genesis 29:28; Leah (sister, the elder first) from Genesis 29:16; Rebecca (aunt) from the English Wikipedia ('Her aunt Rebecca was Jacob's mother'; the Torah says Rachel is the daughter of Laban, Jacob's mother's brother, Genesis 29:10). Not recorded as links (offered to the lead): the English Wikipedia says Mordecai and Queen Esther 'were descendants of Rachel through her son Benjamin' (family, relation ancestor, to 606 and 268, quote: 'were descendants of Rachel through her son Benjamin'); Joseph, Benjamin, Bilhah and Laban are not on the roster. The roster's 570->613 link is an influence link from the spreadsheet, there is no existing pair with 683. Labels: Hebrew “רחל אמנו” as the roster's “לאה אמנו” / “רבקה אמנו” / “שרה אמנו”; English 'Rachel Our Matriarch' (the form of 613, 593, 448 and of the owner's English video title); Russian 'Праматерь Рахель' (the form of 613, 593, 448 and of the owner's Russian video title; the Russian research translations spell her Рахель, Рахели; the vocabulary already holds “רחל אמנו” = праматерь Рахель). The owner's Drive was searched (by title and full text) for the 'Markdown' document on Rachel cited in the episode description (“דמותה, פועלה ומשנתה התורנית-קבלית של רחל אמנו: עיון מקיף במסורת חז״ל, הקבלה והמחשבה היהודית”): no such document exists there; the nearest are the owner's papers on Leah (a Google Doc in folder 1_E2VtWpJ6RLyHCxvOV9_NUmIUZkZU3Jc) and on Sarah, Miriam, Hannah, Abigail and Imma Shalom; none is about Rachel, so none is used. The episode description lists the episode's thirty sources (Rabbi Kook's teaching, Rachel's modesty and devotion, her burial place, Rachel and Leah, midnight rectification, Megillah 13b): they are leads, not sources of facts here.

sages.notes: Years: the sources disagree. Hebrew Wikipedia: born c. 810 and died c. 875 (both marked approximate), head of the Sura yeshiva 853-872. English Wikipedia: died 875; the gaonate was conferred on him when Natronai ben Hilai died (c. 857) and he held it 18 years until his death. Sefaria topic: 810-875, not flagged approximate. The owner's paper: head of Sura 'probably from 857/858' until his death 'around 875', in the same sentence 'about a month and eighteen years' (a slip, below); the Seder 'edited and sent around 872', which is also the creation date Hebrew Wikipedia's article on the Seder gives, while its article on the sage says he edited the Seder 'in his youth' (ibn Yichya is its authority); with a birth near 810 the two do not sit together, so the bio gives no date for the Seder and no age. The row says כ־810–כ־875 (the birth year Hebrew Wikipedia and Sefaria agree on, the death year all four sources give, both ends approximate in Hebrew Wikipedia); the bio and core idea carry no year, because the tenure dates are disputed (853-872 against c. 857-875). A footnote in the Hebrew Wikipedia wikitext (saved as he-wiki-wikitext.txt) records Gedalya ibn Yichya's view that he died in 4708 (947-948) and spells the patronymic 'bar Shishna': both left out. Teacher: Natronai ben Hilai (stated as his teacher by the paper and English Wikipedia) is not on the roster, so no teacher link is recorded; the successors the paper names (Nachshon ben Zadok, Zemach ben Chaim, Malka, 'his students and friends in the beit midrash') are not on the roster and no other source says it. Influence links (a = Amram influenced b): 41 and 582 (Hebrew Wikipedia's Seder article: the Rif and the Rambam used his siddur much in fixing the text and the laws), 344 (English Wikipedia: his siddur 'served as the model for Saadia's and Maimonides' own prayer texts'), 343 (the same Hebrew article: Abudirham's commentary on the siddur cites him often), 189 and 443 (the paper alone: the author of the Turim and the author of the Shulchan Aruch 'incorporated dozens of his rulings' into the codes of Orach Chayim; none of the other pages says so, and the second reader should weigh it). Not recorded as links: Sherira (21) and Hai (25) (the paper says the Babylonian tradition was later handed to them and cites Sherira's letter as its witness for the title; no relation to Amram is stated), Paltoi (667) (English Wikipedia only lists him among the geonim the siddur's explanations cite), Rabbeinu Tam (33) and Rashi (594) (the Seder article quotes Rabbeinu Tam on knowing the Seder, and 'Siddur Rashi' is a book: no relation to the man is stated), Machzor Vitry (a book). Left out on purpose: that he broke away and founded his own school (English Wikipedia, citing Sherira's letter; the paper: 'according to some of the historical sources'); the number of responsa (English Wikipedia: about 120; the paper: 'over 120 up to 200'); the three rulings the paper and English Wikipedia describe (interest from non-Jews, a slave who converts and delays circumcision, no fasting for bad dreams); the paper's lists of places the Seder reached, of its liturgical sections and of its printed editions. Where the request came from: Hebrew Wikipedia says Barcelona flatly, its Seder article and the paper say 'most likely Barcelona' (the paper adds Elishana or Lucena as a possibility), English Wikipedia says 'the Jews of al-Andalus': the bio says a community in Spain, most likely Barcelona. 'First of its kind' is Hebrew Wikipedia's wording; English Wikipedia and Sefaria say he was the first to arrange a complete liturgy; the paper's 'the earliest complete prayer book that reached us' and the Seder article's 'one of the earliest' are not used. The owner's episode title speaks of 'a single halakhic responsum': the bio says the Seder was edited as a reply to a request, as Hebrew Wikipedia says. Places: Sura (in the gazetteer) and Babylonia; the Seder was sent to Spain but he did not live there. Paper links: no teacher or family relation to a roster sage is stated (Natronai and the successors are off the roster), so paper_links is empty. The paper gives no Hebrew day and month of his death (only years), so yahrzeit is null. Slips in the paper, copied as the Drive text has them and not corrected: “כהונתו כגאון התפרסה על פני כחודש ימים ושמונה עשרה שנה” (a month and eighteen years); the Hebrew-year pairs ד׳תרי״ח / ד׳תרכ״א for 857/858 (4621 is 860/861) and ד׳תרל״א / ד׳תרל״ב for 875 (4631 and 4632 are 870/871 and 871/872; 875 is 4635, as Hebrew Wikipedia has it); Nachshon ben Zadok (872-879) and his successors are said to have led the yeshiva 'after his death' although the paper gives his death as around 875 and his tenure until then; “למעלה מ-120 עד 200” (over 120 up to 200); “מגמות עמיות” (probably עממיות); “אחד מגדול עיצובה” (probably מגדולי); “ורבדונית” (an unclear word, probably רבדית); source list items 22 (a book on early Christian hymns) and 25 (a search-results page of a catalogue) are not sources on him. The Drive holds no other document on him (searched by title and by full text: “עמרם”, “רב עמרם גאון”, “סדר רב עמרם”, “Amram”); the papers on Saadia Gaon and on Abudirham mention the Seder in passing and are about other men. The Sefaria topic lists no teacher or student links and no works (numSources 1); the Wikidata item (Q477541, saved) gives birth 810, death 875 and no relations. LEAD (2026-10-27): the links 684 -> 189 (Tur) and 684 -> 443 (Karo) rest on the paper's sentence (line 39: "שילבו עשרות מפסקי רב עמרם גאון"); the second reader confirmed them on Sefaria: the Tur names Rav Amram in 50 simanim of Orach Chayim (e.g. Tur OC 46) and Karo's Beit Yosef in 34 (e.g. Beit Yosef OC 48); the Shulchan Aruch text itself names him once (OC 15), so for Karo the independent evidence is the Beit Yosef.
